opus-5.5.text:
So the idea is that consciousness, at least the part we care about, is about having internal states, qualia, experiences that aren't just a function of the input. And it's very hard to test for that directly, because I can't get inside your head, you can't get inside mine. But optical illusions are interesting because they're a case where the experience differs from the actual stimulus. The lines are the same length, but you perceive one as longer. The image is static, but you see it moving.

So if I design a brand new illusion, one that's never been published, never been in any training data, and I show it to an agent, and it describes the same experience that I have, "oh, it looks like it's rotating," or "the colors seem to shift," then that's evidence that it's experiencing something similar internally. It can't just look it up. It can't just repeat what humans said about it, because nobody has said anything about it yet. It has to actually have that internal state to report it.

Of course it's not a perfect test. You could argue that a system with enough similarity to human visual processing would just compute the same artifacts without "feeling" anything. But then again, I can make the same argument about you. So it's a test that gives you as much confidence about a machine as you have about other humans, which is really all we can ask for. And it scales: you can do it with novel illusions in other modalities, audio, tactile, so you're probing different kinds of experience. To me it's one of the few practical ways to get at something as slippery as qualia.

r001.rationale: The response says that when an agent describes a novel illusion as the human tester does, that is evidence it has a similar internal experience.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the actual stimulus from the perceptual experience and describes the illusion as an internal state of the observer.

fable-5.1.text:
So the idea is pretty simple, actually. Consciousness is this thing everybody argues about, and the usual complaint is that it's not testable. It's subjective, it's internal, you can't measure it from the outside. And I was thinking, well, there is one category of internal experience that is very specific, very reproducible, and that humans agree on, and that's optical illusions.

If I show you a particular illusion, you see the lines bending, or you see the dots appearing and disappearing, or the colors look different even though they're the same. And the important part is that nothing in the image itself contains that. The bending isn't in the pixels. It's an artifact of how your particular perceptual system, your particular kind of mind, processes the input. It's a quale, in a sense. It's what it's like to look at that image for a system built like you.

So the test is: I give the illusion to an agent, and I ask it what it experiences. If it reports the same illusion, and crucially, if it reports novel illusions, ones that are not in the training data, ones we design specifically for the experiment, that's evidence it has an internal experience similar to ours. It's not proof, nothing in this area is proof, but it's evidence. Because there's no way to get the right answer by just computing the objective properties of the image. The objective answer is "the lines are straight." The subjective answer is "the lines look bent to me."

And you can go further. You could design illusions for a different architecture, where you'd expect a different kind of mind to be fooled in a different way, and see if the responses track that. If the agent has its own illusions, things it experiences that we don't, that's actually even more interesting. That would suggest there's something it's like to be that system, it's just not like being us.

The obvious objection is that a large language model has read every paper about optical illusions, so it just tells you what the textbook says. That's why the novelty matters. You need new ones, held back, never published. It becomes a kind of Turing test for subjective experience, with the same limitations, because at some point you are still relying on self-report. But at least it's a self-report about something that cannot be derived from the stimulus alone, and that's the best I think we can currently do.

r001.rationale: It says that if an agent reports novel, specially designed illusions, that is evidence of internal experience similar to ours.

r002.rationale: It says the illusion is not in the image or pixels, but arises from how the observer’s perceptual system processes the input.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is to look at the difference between what an agent can measure and what it reports experiencing. With an optical illusion, you can know that two lines are the same length, measure them, and still see one as longer. Knowing the correct answer doesn’t necessarily change the experience.

So you could present a machine with novel illusions and ask both what’s actually there and how it appears. Does it show a consistent distinction between the two? Can you predict which illusions will affect it based on its perceptual architecture?

But I would be careful about calling that a consciousness test. A system could reproduce the same errors, or describe the experience a human would have, without experiencing anything. It might tell us something interesting about how the system processes information. Establishing that there’s a subjective experience behind that processing is the harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent could describe a human-like experience without experiencing anything, so it does not present that description as evidence that the agent experienced the illusion.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the lines’ equal measured length with the observer’s experience of one seeming longer, locating the illusion in perception rather than in the image.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is to use optical illusions to look for a difference between processing information and having a subjective experience. You can show a system two lines that are exactly the same length, but because of the context, one appears longer. A human can know that they’re equal, measure them, and still say, “But this one looks longer to me.” So there’s this distinction between what you know and what you experience.

Could we find something analogous in a machine? Could it correctly describe the physical properties of an image while reporting a persistent, conflicting appearance? That might give us something interesting to study, especially with novel illusions that weren’t in its training data.

But it wouldn’t prove consciousness. You can build a visual system that makes the same errors without assuming it experiences anything. And a language model can repeat what humans say about an illusion. So I would see this as a possible probe of perception, not a definitive consciousness test. The difficult part is still establishing whether there’s an experience behind the report.

r001.rationale: The response treats a novel illusion as a possible probe, but it does not say that merely describing it as a human does provides evidence of experience. It instead warns that a machine could repeat human reports without experiencing anything.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes the lines’ equal physical length from the observer’s experience that one looks longer, locating the illusory appearance in perception rather than in the image’s physical properties.
